facts.statement: Galahadosuchus is a genus of saltoposuchid crocodylomorph that lived in the Late Triassic.
facts.quote: A member of Crocodylomorpha belonging to the family Saltoposuchidae.

facts.statement: Galahadosuchus fossils come from the Late Triassic fissure deposits of Cromhall Quarry in the United Kingdom.
facts.quote: Galahadosuchus is an extinct genus of saltoposuchid crocodylomorph from the Late Triassic fissure deposits of Cromhall Quarry in the United Kingdom.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen NHMUK PV R 10002 was recovered by Ron Croucher in 1969 from site 1 of the Cromhall Quarry fissure deposits.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Galahadosuchus, NHMUK PV R 10002, was recovered by Ron Croucher in 1969 from site 1 of the fissure deposits at Cromhall Quarry in Gloucestershire, southwest England.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Galahadosuchus may have been faster than the closely related Terrestrisuchus and possessed more flexible hands.
facts.quote: some subtle anatomical differences might suggest that the two taxa differed slightly in their locomotion, with Galahadosuchus possibly having been a faster animal with more flexible hands.

facts.statement: A distinctive feature of Galahadosuchus is its relatively short and stout ulnare and radiale, each about one‑tenth the length of the corresponding forearm bones.
facts.quote: Each bone is at most only a tenth the length of their respective limb bone pairing in the forearm, i.e. radius plus humerus for the radiale and ulna plus humerus for the ulnare.

facts.statement: Within Saltoposuchidae, the basal member is Saltoposuchus, while Litargosuchus is the immediate sister to the Galahadosuchus‑Terrestrisuchus clade in some analyses.
facts.quote: In the resulting tree, the immediate sister form to both Galahadosuchus and Terrestrisuchus is Litargosuchus, with Saltoposuchus as the family's basalmost member.

facts.statement: The femur’s medially directed head indicates an erect stance by restricting hindlimb movement to the parasagittal plane.
facts.quote: The shape of the femur meanwhile, with its distinct medially directed head, indicates an erect stance, as this morphology restricts the hindlimbs movement to the parasagittal plane, therefore setting it apart from the more sprawling stance taken on by modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: In limb‑proportion analyses Galahadosuchus clusters with quadrupedal forms but plots slightly closer to bipedal taxa than Terrestrisuchus.
facts.quote: they were found to still cluster with other quadrupedal forms, but slightly closer to bipedal forms than Terrestrisuchus.

facts.statement: Elongated proximal carpals are thought to support body weight, whereas Galahadosuchus’s shorter, more robust radiale and ulnare may have made its hand more flexible than that of its relatives.
facts.quote: The elongated proximal carpals of early crocodylomorphs are thought to be an adaptation to bearing the animal′s weight, forming a single functional unit. Contrasting this, the shorter, more robust radiale and ulnare of Galahadosuchus might have had the opposite effect, making the hand more flexible than those of its relatives.

facts.statement: Shortened first and fifth metacarpals suggest that the outer digits did not bear weight, with only the middle three digits supporting the animal on the ground.
facts.quote: The shortened first metacarpal seen in both Galahadosuchus and Terrestrisuchus likely means that the matching digit was likewise shorter, something which has been interpreted as a sign that this particular finger did not bear the animal′s weight when on the ground. The fact that the same shortening appears to be present in the fifth metacarpal would then suggest that neither the first nor last digit of the hands were actually weight-bearing, only the middle three.

facts.statement: The holotype NHMUK PV R 10002 from the Late Triassic fissure deposits of Cromhall Quarry was designated as Galahadosuchus jonesi n. gen. n. sp.
